analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus genomic surveillance faces distributed data, heterogeneity, and limited expert capacity (A1). title: Differentiating Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) andHemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) Using a Stacking Ensemble

analysis.background: Distinguishing Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) from Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) is challenging once organ‑specific signs appear, delaying timely clinical decisions.
analysis.methods: The authors generated 8,000 synthetic records with 22 symptom features, applied binary encoding and SMOTE within 5‑fold stratified cross‑validation, and trained a stacking ensemble of XGBoost and LightGBM base learners with Logistic Regression as meta‑learner.

title: Distribution and richness of Orthohantavirus reservoir hosts: Implications for zoonotic risk in Southern South America.

analysis.background: Orthohantaviruses represent a major zoonotic threat in Southern South America, with 13 native rodent species recognized as reservoirs of 15 viral genotypes, and existing distribution information is fragmented, limiting risk assessment.
analysis.methods: The authors compiled and curated occurrence records for reservoir hosts, used ecological niche modeling to estimate potential distributions, integrated binary presence predictions to map reservoir and genotype richness, and combined richness maps with gridded human population data to estimate the number of people potentially exposed.
analysis.results: Most reservoir species are predicted across eastern and northeastern Argentina, parts of Paraguay, Uruguay, and southern Brazil; hotspots of reservoir richness are concentrated in the Humid Chaco, while high genotype richness extends across the Chaco‑Pampean plain; exposure to ≥7 pathogenic genotypes is estimated to exceed 13 million people under the most precautionary scenario.
analysis.contribution: This study provides the first integrated, region‑wide assessment of Orthohantavirus reservoir distributions and richness in Southern South America, offering an updated ecological baseline to support surveillance, risk mapping, and prevention strategies.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available; detailed methods, validation, sample sizes, and uncertainty estimates are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Orthohantaviruses are a major zoonotic threat in Southern South America, with 13 rodent reservoirs for 15 genotypes and fragmented distribution data. title: Serologic Evidence of Hantavirus Exposure in Humans, Italy, 2004–2018

analysis.background: Rodent‑borne hantaviruses and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) circulate in northern Italy but are rarely diagnosed.
analysis.methods: The study tested serum from 371 patients collected 2004–2018 in the provinces of Novara, Biella, Vercelli, and Verbano‑Cusio‑Ossola; IgG against PUUV, DOBV and LCMV was screened by immunofluorescence assay, and samples with titers >1:40 were further examined by focus‑reduction neutralization tests in Vero E6 cells.

analysis.contribution: The work provides the first serologic evidence of hantavirus and LCMV exposure in northwestern Italy, highlighting under‑recognition of these zoonoses in a region previously lacking data.
analysis.limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Rodent‑borne hantaviruses and LCMV circulate in northern Italy but are rarely diagnosed. Methods: Serum from 371 patients (2004–2018) in four provinces was screened for hantavirus and LCMV IgG by immunofluorescence, with high‑titer samples further tested by focus‑reduction neutralization in Vero E6 cells. Results: Hantavirus IgG was detected in 7.3% (27/371) and LCMV IgG in 2.7% (10/371); PUUV‑neutralizing antibodies were confirmed in 10 of 11 hantavirus‑positive samples, showing local PUUV circulation. Contribution: This is the first serologic evidence of hantavirus and LCMV exposure in northwestern Italy, revealing under‑diagnosis. Limitations: Not reported in the supplied evidence.

title: 2026 Cruise Ship-associated Andes Hantavirus Outbreak and Public Health Response.

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) uniquely exhibits repeated human-to-human transmission and causes severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with high lethality in South America (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review synthesizes epidemiological and clinical features, transmission routes, and patterns of spread in a confined, high-density setting, using the 2026 MV Hondius cruise‑ship outbreak as a case study (A2).
analysis.current_state: Genomic sequencing showed ≤1 SNP difference among cases, supporting a single or few zoonotic introductions followed by onboard human-to-human spread, with an estimated effective reproduction number of 0.7 (A7).
analysis.gaps: The analysis relies on publicly available reports and limited case numbers, leaving uncertainties about the full spectrum of risk factors, asymptomatic infection rates, and the robustness of R0 estimates (A3).
analysis.future_research: Future work should institutionalize travel-history screening, strengthen surveillance for suspected hantavirus cases, and expand rapid diagnostic capacity, alongside studies of transmission dynamics in closed environments (A11).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus uniquely transmits between humans and causes lethal cardiopulmonary syndrome (A1). Main directions: The review collates epidemiology, clinical presentation, and transmission in a high‑density cruise‑ship setting (A2). Current state: Genomic data indicate ≤1 SNP difference among cases, suggesting a single spillover followed by limited human‑to‑human spread with R0≈0.7 (A7). Gaps: Reliance on public reports and few cases creates uncertainty about risk factors, asymptomatic rates, and R0 precision (A3). Future research: Implement routine travel‑history checks, enhance hantavirus surveillance, expand rapid diagnostics, and study transmission in confined environments (A11).

title: Spectrum of Gastrointestinal, Hepatobiliary, and Pancreatic Involvement in Hantavirus Infection: A Narrative Review.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a rodent‑borne zoonosis causing hemorrhagic fever with renal failure and pulmonary syndrome, recently highlighted by outbreaks. Future research: Prospective large‑scale studies are needed to clarify pathogenesis, frequency, risk stratification, and optimal management of these manifestations.
